approved: Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (2014 Budget Measures No. 2) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would change multiple social security and family payment rules as part of the 2014 Budget.
It would pause indexation of certain payment limits, reset deeming thresholds, and limit overseas portability for disability support pension.
From 1 July 2025, the qualifying age for age pension would increase to 70 years, rising by six months every two years.
Pause indexation of income free areas and asset limits for student payments for three years from January 2015.
Pause indexation of income and asset test free areas for most pensioners for three years from July 2017.
Index all pensions only to the Consumer Price Index from 20 September 2017.
Reset deeming thresholds to $30,000 for singles, $50,000 for couples, and $25,000 for couple members from 20 September 2017.
Limit disability support pension overseas portability to 28 days per 12 months from 1 January 2015.
Increase age pension qualifying age to 70 years from 1 July 2025.
Recipients of social security payments, family payments, and veterans' entitlements, including students, pensioners, and families.

Moved the day's final debate management motion, capping debate on two Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment budget bills at 3 hours for the second reading and 30 minutes for consideration in detail, to pass them to the Senate by week's end.

Opposed the Social Services budget bills, citing Australian Council of Social Service modelling that pensioners will be $80 a week worse off within a decade, and NATSEM analysis showing about 1.2 million families will be on average $3,000 a year worse off by 2017-18, while the government proceeds with a $22 billion Paid Parental Leave scheme.

Opposed the Social Services budget bills, noting Australia's welfare spending is just 8.6 per cent of GDP compared with an OECD average of 13 per cent, and calculated that job seekers aged 22 to 24 moved from Newstart to Youth Allowance would lose about $48 a week, an 18 per cent income cut.

Defended the Social Services budget bills, projecting they would reduce debt from a forecast $667 billion to $389 billion within a decade, warned Australia's worker-to-pensioner support ratio will fall to about 2.7 to one by mid-century, and noted a review of a rule that let disability pensioners travel overseas for 19 weeks while still receiving payments.

Opposed the Social Services bills, calculating that changing pension indexation would leave a single pensioner in his Charlton electorate about $1,500 a year worse off over four years, and contrasted the $50,000 Paid Parental Leave payment available in wealthier electorates with the under $20,000 that more than 80 per cent of Charlton women would receive.

Opposed the Social Services bills, noting 29,995 families in his McEwen electorate receive family tax benefits that would be cut, quoted a self-described Liberal-voting Puckapunyal chaplain's constituent email warning of harm to volunteer-reliant single-income families, and cited National Seniors Australia's Michael O'Neill on retirees' inability to absorb sudden bill spikes.

Defended the Social Services bills, breaking down the $415 billion 2014-15 budget to show $146 billion goes to social security, including $42 billion for income support for seniors alone, and cited an estimate that each month of delay in passing these measures would cost taxpayers more than $117 million.

Moved a package of opposition amendments to both Social Services budget bills, seeking to strip out measures including changes to pension indexation, the pension age increase and family tax benefit freezes, but declined to elaborate given the government's gag motion limiting debate time.
